title: Julius Caesar
author: William Shakespeare
openingText: FLAVIUS. Get off the streets! Go home, you lazy creatures, go home. Is this a holiday? Don't you know that as working men you shouldn't walk around on a workday without the marks of your trade? Speak up — what's your trade?
about:
Julius Caesar is a play about political assassination and its aftermath. Brutus, a Roman senator and Caesar's friend, is persuaded by Cassius and other conspirators that Caesar's growing power threatens the republic. They murder Caesar on the steps of the Senate on the Ides of March. What follows is not triumph but catastrophe: Antony's funeral oration turns the Roman crowd against the assassins, civil war erupts, and Brutus and Cassius die at the Battle of Philippi. The play's title is Caesar, but its center is Brutus — a man who kills his friend for the public good and discovers that the public good is not so easily served.

Written around 1599, probably just before Hamlet, Julius Caesar was one of the first plays performed at the newly built Globe Theatre. It draws on Plutarch's Lives and is Shakespeare's most direct engagement with republican politics — the question of when, if ever, it is justified to overthrow a ruler. The play refuses to settle the question. Caesar is arrogant but not a tyrant; Brutus is honorable but wrong about the consequences; Antony is opportunistic but effective. Shakespeare gives every position its strongest voice and lets the audience decide. The result is a play that has been claimed by revolutionaries and conservatives alike for four centuries — and that speaks to any moment when political violence is debated.

angleCards.title: Was the assassination justified?
angleCards.text: Shakespeare gives Brutus real reasons — Caesar's ambition, the threat to the republic — and shows that acting on those reasons produces catastrophe. The play does not answer the question; it forces you to hold both truths at once.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Julius Caesar as a test case for political violence — to weigh whether Brutus was right to kill Caesar and what the consequences tell us about the ethics of assassination.

angleCards.title: The power of rhetoric.
angleCards.text: Brutus speaks in reasoned prose; Antony speaks in emotional verse. Both address the same crowd after the same event, and Antony wins. Track the two funeral orations as a study in how language moves people — and whether the better argument is the one that wins.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the play as a study of rhetoric and persuasion — to compare Brutus's appeal to reason with Antony's appeal to emotion and to understand why emotion wins.

angleCards.title: Brutus as the tragic figure.
angleCards.text: The play is called Julius Caesar but it belongs to Brutus. He is the only character who acts from principle rather than self-interest, and his principled action destroys everything he meant to protect. Watch how Shakespeare makes his nobility the source of his failure.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow Brutus as the play's real protagonist — to understand how his honor and his misjudgment are the same quality, and why the noblest character produces the worst outcome.

angleCards.title: The mob.
angleCards.text: The Roman crowd cheers Brutus, then cheers Antony, then murders an innocent poet because he shares a name with a conspirator. Shakespeare's portrait of the crowd is the play's darkest element — and its most relevant to democratic politics.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to pay attention to the crowd — how easily it is swayed, how quickly it turns violent — and to read Shakespeare's portrait of the Roman mob as a warning about popular politics.

cast.name: Brutus
cast.description: A Roman senator, respected by all, who joins the conspiracy against Caesar out of genuine concern for the republic rather than personal ambition. He is the play's moral center and its most complete failure — a man whose every principled decision produces a worse outcome than the unprincipled alternative would have. Shakespeare makes him sympathetic and wrong at the same time.

cast.name: Julius Caesar
cast.description: The most powerful man in Rome, recently returned from military triumph, offered the crown three times by Antony and three times refusing it. He is proud, deaf in one ear, superstitious, and aware that men around him might wish him dead. He appears in fewer scenes than the title suggests; his assassination in Act 3 is the fulcrum of the play, and his ghost haunts the rest of it.

cast.name: Mark Antony
cast.description: Caesar's loyal friend, initially dismissed by the conspirators as a mere follower. His funeral oration — 'Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears' — is the most famous speech in Shakespeare and the play's decisive turning point. He is politically shrewd, emotionally volatile, and ruthless once he has the crowd behind him.

cast.name: Cassius
cast.description: The driving force behind the conspiracy, motivated by personal envy as much as political principle. He is a keen reader of other men — it is Cassius who recruits Brutus, knowing that the conspiracy needs Brutus's reputation to succeed. He is the more practical of the two leaders and is overruled by Brutus at every critical decision, to their mutual destruction.

cast.name: Portia
cast.description: Brutus's wife, who senses his inner turmoil and demands to know what conspiracy he is hiding. She wounds herself in the thigh to prove she can bear pain and keep secrets. Her death — reported later in the play — is one of the costs of the assassination that Brutus bears in private.

cast.name: Calpurnia
cast.description: Caesar's wife, who dreams of his murder the night before the Ides of March and begs him not to go to the Senate. Caesar almost listens — then is persuaded otherwise by the conspirators. Her warning is the play's clearest signal that the assassination could have been avoided.

whyItMatters.title: The Politics of Assassination
whyItMatters.body: Julius Caesar is the Western canon's most sustained dramatic examination of political assassination — and its judgment is neither simple nor settled. Shakespeare gives Brutus real reasons to kill Caesar and shows that the killing produces outcomes worse than what it was meant to prevent. The play has been staged as a warning against tyranny and as a warning against those who would overthrow tyrants; it has been performed in revolutionary contexts from eighteenth-century America to twentieth-century dictatorships. Its power comes from its refusal to choose sides: it takes the assassin's motives seriously and the assassination's consequences seriously, and it asks the audience to hold both without the comfort of a clear verdict. Every subsequent debate about political violence — its justification, its limits, its unintended consequences — is in conversation with this play.

whyItMatters.title: The Funeral Orations
whyItMatters.body: Brutus's speech to the crowd after the assassination — rational, principled, appealing to the citizens' love of liberty — and Antony's response — emotional, insinuating, wielding Caesar's bloody mantle and his will — are together the most famous study of rhetoric in English literature. Brutus explains; Antony performs. Brutus addresses the mind; Antony addresses the gut. Antony wins, and the crowd that cheered Brutus five minutes earlier now wants to burn his house down. The scene is Shakespeare's most direct statement about how political persuasion actually works — not through argument but through feeling, not through truth but through performance — and it has never been more relevant than in an age of mass media and political spectacle.

whyItMatters.title: The Noble Failure
whyItMatters.body: Brutus is Shakespeare's portrait of a good man in politics — and the play's argument that goodness is not enough. He joins the conspiracy for the best reasons and makes every subsequent decision on principle rather than calculation: he refuses to kill Antony, he allows Antony to speak at the funeral, he insists on marching to Philippi rather than waiting. Each decision is honorable. Each is catastrophic. Shakespeare is not mocking Brutus's virtue; he is showing that virtue without political realism is a recipe for disaster. The play's tragic force comes from the recognition that the most principled person in the room is also the one whose principles destroy everything he was trying to save.
